title: Arun Mehta vs. Sunrise Properties — Security Deposit Refund
factsSummary: Arun Mehta rented an apartment from Sunrise Properties under a 24-month lease agreement ending July 2025. He paid a security deposit of ₹1,20,000. Upon vacating after the lease expiry, he requested the deposit refund as per the lease terms. The landlord refused, citing vague 'damages to the property' without providing any inspection report, photographs, or repair bills. The tenant documented the move-out condition with timestamped photographs showing the property in good condition. A legal notice was sent on 15 August 2025 demanding the refund, which was ignored.

applicableProvisions: Section 43 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 — Recovery of possession and deposit refund
Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract

assessment.legalDirectionExplanation: The tenant has a clear contractual right to the deposit refund under the lease agreement. The landlord's refusal citing damages is unsupported by any evidence. The tenant has timestamped move-out photographs contradicting the damage claim. The burden of proof lies on the landlord under Section 43 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act.

title: Neha Kapoor vs. Vikram Singh — Unpaid Personal Loan Recovery
factsSummary: Neha Kapoor lent ₹5,00,000 to her friend Vikram Singh on 20 January 2025 for his business expansion. A promissory note was signed by the defendant. The defendant made two monthly repayments of ₹25,000 each via bank transfer in February and March 2025, then stopped. When the plaintiff demanded repayment, the defendant claimed the amount was a 'gift' and not a loan. The promissory note exists but no independent witnesses were present during the transaction. WhatsApp messages show the defendant acknowledging the debt initially but later changing his stance.

evidence.description: Statement showing ₹5,00,000 transfer from plaintiff to defendant's account

evidence.description: Bank statements showing ₹25,000 repayments in Feb and Mar 2025

Defendant apologised for delay, promised to resume repayment next month
Defendant first mentioned the amount might have been a 'gift'
Plaintiff sent formal repayment demand with breakup of outstanding amount

applicableProvisions: Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Promissory note definition and enforceability
Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Promise in writing and registered

assessment.legalDirectionExplanation: The plaintiff has a signed promissory note and bank transfer records establishing the transfer of funds. However, the absence of independent witnesses and the defendant's claim that it was a 'gift' create factual disputes. The partial repayments support the loan theory, but Section 25(3) requires a written promise to repay, which the promissory note satisfies. The outcome will heavily depend on the court's assessment of credibility.

title: Ravi Desai vs. Apex Constructions — Breach of Service Contract
factsSummary: Ravi Desai, an interior designer, verbally agreed with Apex Constructions to provide design and project management services for a commercial office space. The scope of work was discussed informally over meetings and WhatsApp messages. No written contract was signed. The plaintiff provided initial designs, vendor coordination, and site supervision over 6 weeks. A cost estimate of ₹3,50,000 was shared via WhatsApp. The defendant made an initial payment of ₹50,000 but stopped payments midway, claiming the work was substandard and incomplete. The plaintiff ceased work after non-payment. The scope, timeline, and quality standards were never formally documented.

evidence.description: Chats discussing scope, cost estimate of ₹3,50,000, and design approvals

evidence.name: Work Photographs
evidence.description: Photos of completed design work and site supervision

evidence.description: Invoice for ₹3,50,000 raised by plaintiff and shared with defendant

evidence.description: Bank statement showing initial payment from defendant

witnesses.statement: Was present during the initial discussion but scope details were vague and informal

Plaintiff shared design concepts and mood boards
Defendant approved initial designs, asked to proceed
Defendant complained about quality of work, refused to pay balance
Plaintiff sent formal demand for outstanding payment of ₹3,00,000

applicableProvisions: Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — What agreements are contracts
Section 36 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Effect of failure to perform at fixed time

assessment.legalDirectionExplanation: The absence of a written contract creates fundamental evidentiary problems. The scope of work, timeline, deliverables, and quality standards were never formally documented. WhatsApp messages and oral discussions are insufficient to establish the precise terms of the contract. The defendant's counterclaim of substandard work cannot be effectively rebutted without objective quality benchmarks. Courts are significantly less likely to enforce vague or oral agreements for professional services.
